questions.q: According to E.M. Forster in "The Story", what is the fundamental difference between a 'story' and the 'finer growths' of a novel?
questions.a: A story is a narrative of events arranged in their time-sequence (e.g., dinner after breakfast, Tuesday after Monday) and has only one merit: making the audience want to know what happens next. The "finer growths" are the nobler aspects the story supports — value, character, morality, perception of truth — which constitute the "life by values" measured by intensity, not minutes. A wrong answer (e.g., "story is the theme" or "story includes character") reveals confusion between the raw chronological backbone and the artistic organism the novel becomes.

questions.q: Forster writes: "Daily life... is practically composed of two lives — the life in time and the life by values." Explain in your own words what he means by "life by values" and give one example from your own experience.
questions.a: "Life by values" refers to moments measured by emotional intensity or significance rather than clock-time — e.g., "I only saw her for five minutes, but it was worth it." The five minutes is clock-time; the "worth it" is value-time where a brief moment piles up into a pinnacle in memory. A wrong answer (e.g., "values means moral values" or "it means the plot") shows the student hasn't grasped Forster's distinction between chronological duration and psychological intensity.

questions.q: Apply Forster's concept: In a novel you have read, identify a scene where the author disrupts chronological order (e.g., flashback, flash-forward, slowed time). Explain what thematic purpose this disruption serves — does it create suspense, reveal character psychology, or emphasize a value-moment?
questions.a: Example: In *Wuthering Heights*, Brontë begins near the end (Lockwood at Wuthering Heights), then Nelly narrates the past. This disruption creates mystery (suspense) and mirrors the haunting of the past on the present — a "value-moment" where past intensity overrides chronology. A weak answer merely lists the disruption without linking to Forster's "double allegiance" or thematic effect.

questions.q: Forster compares the story to a "backbone — or may I say a tape-worm." Analyze this metaphor: what does each comparison suggest about the nature of story in a novel? Why does he offer two images?
questions.a: "Backbone" suggests structural necessity — the story supports the novel's body (finer growths). "Tape-worm" suggests something parasitic, wriggling, interminable, arbitrary in beginning/end, and "unlovely and dull" when isolated. The dual metaphor captures Forster's ambivalence: story is structurally indispensable yet artistically low. A wrong answer (e.g., "both mean the same") misses the critical nuance of his attitude toward plot.

questions.q: Evaluate Forster's claim: "It is never possible for a novelist to deny time inside the fabric of his novel." Consider Sterne's *Tristram Shandy* (time upside down) and Proust (simultaneous supper and nursery). Do these experiments "contravene" his thesis or prove it? Justify.
questions.a: They prove it. Even when Sterne turns the clock upside down or Proust alters the hands, the clock (time-sequence) still exists — the reader must reconstruct chronology to understand. The devices are legitimate *because* they play against a recognized temporal framework. A wrong answer (e.g., "they disprove him because time is broken") fails to see that subversion requires a norm to subvert.

questions.q: Create a micro-narrative (3-4 sentences) that demonstrates Forster's "double allegiance": include a clear chronological sequence (life in time) AND a moment where intensity distorts time-perception (life by values). Label each part.
questions.a: [Life in time] The train left at 6:00, reached at 8:00, and I walked home by 8:15. [Life by values] But the five minutes on the platform when she said goodbye stretched into a year — I still hear the whistle in that silence. A poor answer writes only chronological events or only emotional reflection without the juxtaposition.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Plot?
questions.a: Students confuse "story" (Forster's term for raw chronological sequence) with "plot" (causal/logical structure) and think Forster is discussing plot when he defines story.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can distinguish between story (chronological events) and plot (causal/logical sequence), identify the structural components of a narrative using Forster's concepts of "life in time" vs "life by values", and explain how narrative structure manipulates temporal order to create suspense, irony, or thematic depth in a board-exam.
